issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette:
Garrett Holloway is a 49-year-old married man of European descent who serves as a city council member in a mid-sized Midwestern municipality. He presented for psychological evaluation approximately eighteen months after returning from a reserve deployment to a combat zone, carrying a PCL-5 score of 42 and a wariness in his posture that made even the intake waiting room seem, to him, like a space that required monitoring.

Garrett had served in the Army Reserve for over two decades, deploying twice in his thirties without lasting psychological consequence - or so he had believed. His third deployment, at 47, was different. During a convoy escort mission, the vehicle ahead of his was struck by an IED. He was close enough to feel the pressure wave move through his chest before he registered the sound. He dismounted and moved toward the wreckage, and what he encountered there - the smoke, the heat against his hands, the sounds of the men - left him with a fragmented internal record that he has never been able to assemble into a coherent sequence. He knows what he did. He does not know, in any continuous way, what he experienced. When he tries to explain it - to his wife, to his physician, to himself - he loses the thread somewhere in the middle and cannot find his way back to the end. What returns instead is not memory in any ordinary sense but the terror itself, arriving without narrative, as if the interval between then and now had simply collapsed.

In the months after his return, Garrett resumed his council duties, attending budget hearings, constituent meetings, and public forums. It was in these settings that the first signs of disruption became impossible to ignore. A colleague who clapped him on the shoulder during a corridor conversation sent him lurching backward, heart hammering, hand raised before he had consciously registered the touch. He began positioning himself at the end of rows and near exits. He had come to understand his own body as something unreliable - a system that continued to issue emergency signals regardless of what his rational mind could verify about his surroundings. When constituents or colleagues assured him that a tense public meeting was over, that things were under control, that he was among friends, he found it genuinely impossible to absorb that information as true. The assurance would land and then dissolve, leaving the same ambient sense of unresolved danger.

At home, Garrett began sleeping with the television on, volume high enough to fill the room. He told himself it helped him stay present, and in a narrow sense it did - the noise occupied enough of his attention that the internal monitoring quieted slightly. He had taken to watching his own thoughts with the vigilance of someone expecting to find something alarming in them, scanning for what he privately feared was evidence that he was losing coherence, losing the boundary between the man he had been and whatever the convoy had made of him. He had come to believe that the world was, in a fundamental and non-negotiable sense, dangerous - not as a political position but as a bodily conviction that preceded any reasoning he could apply to it. He was on guard at all the time, and he could not locate the off switch.

Physical contact with others had become something he actively avoided. His wife, Denise, had adapted without either of them discussing it directly, and the distance that had opened between them over fourteen months had become its own kind of presence in the house. She had stopped reaching for him. He had noticed her stopping, and had felt both relieved and ashamed of the relief.

What finally brought Garrett to seek help was a council session in which a constituent, leaning across the dais to make a point, briefly touched his forearm. The alarm response that followed was visible enough that a colleague asked afterward whether he was all right. He said yes. That evening, he told Denise he needed to talk to someone. What he is most afraid of, sitting across from a clinician for the first time, is that what is happening inside him cannot be explained - and that if it could be, the explanation would confirm what he most fears about himself.
